land.text: British Nigeria, independent from the United Kingdom on 1 October 1960; the Northern Cameroons joined in 1961

predecessors.note: Cliopatria draws Nigeria in 1957-1960 (the years checked) inside its 'British Gold Coast' row (modern Nigeria, Ghana and Cameroon cells, 1.19 M km2 to 1959 and 0.95 M km2 in 1960), not inside 'British Africa'. The Northern Cameroons were a British-administered territory that joined after the 1961 plebiscite.

capitals.name: Lagos
capitals.note: The Abuja page says Abuja 'replaced Lagos ... as the capital on 12 December 1991'; it does not say in a separate sentence that Lagos was the capital from 1960, which is implied. The Nigeria page lists Lagos only as the largest city.

capitals.name: Abuja
capitals.note: Capital 'on 12 December 1991'; Decree No. 6 of 4 February 1976 began the move from Lagos. Coordinates 9 deg 4' N, 7 deg 29' E from the page.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Nigeria shape begins in 1961; in 1960 it draws the land inside its British Gold Coast row (3,879 of the 3,883 cells). The Northern Cameroons strip along the eastern border is a gazetteer name still to be added.

correction.text: the shape as drawn, including the Northern Cameroons from 1961; from 30 May 1967 the Eastern Region is Biafra's and is carved out by the ledger's loss, occupation and gain events until 15 January 1970

keyframe_review.note: 0.911 M km2 against the infobox's 923,769 km2 (ratio 0.99). The page dates the Northern Cameroons' joining only to the 1961 plebiscite year, which agrees with the shape's 1961 start. The 1961-1968 and 1969-2023 shapes are identical to 0.01 percent; no border move between them is on the pages opened. Bakassi (ceded to Cameroon in 2008) is not on the Nigeria page and is not removed here.

correction.text: the shape as drawn, except that until 15 January 1970 the Biafran remainder of the Eastern Region is not under Nigerian control

keyframe_review.note: 0.911 M km2. The civil war lasted 'from 6 July 1967 to 15 January 1970' (infobox), so the 1969 shape over-draws Nigeria for the first fortnight of 1970. Cliopatria has no Biafra polity; a rebel dossier is needed (see notes).
Same outline as 1969 at 0.911 M km2. The Nigeria page lists land borders with Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon and a shared Lake Chad water boundary, but no later change.

region.text: Nigeria at independence, before the Northern Cameroons joined

ledger.note: 1 October 1960: Nigeria becomes independent. It 'gained full independence from the United Kingdom on 1 October 1960'.

1961: the Northern Cameroons join Nigeria. 'Southern Cameroons opted to join the Republic of Cameroon while Northern Cameroons chose to join Nigeria.' The Nigeria page gives only the 1961 plebiscite year; the British Cameroons page dates the union: the plebiscite was 'held on 11 February 1961' and 'Northern Cameroons became the Sardauna Province of Northern Nigeria on 1 June 1961' (month added by the af-08-h reviewer).
1 October 1963: Nigeria becomes a republic. Infobox: 'Became a republic: 1 October 1963.' The state continues; only the form changes.

region.text: the Eastern Region, which Ojukwu 'renamed ... the Republic of Biafra' (modern states Abia, Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bayelsa, Cross River, Ebonyi, Enugu, Imo and Rivers: the researcher's mapping)

ledger.note: 30 May 1967: Biafra secedes. 'On 30 May 1967, Ojukwu declared independence and renamed the entire Eastern Region "the Republic of Biafra"'; on 27 May Gowon's decree had split the region into three states. The region is the page's; the admin-1 mapping is the researcher's.

region.text: the Mid-Western state (modern Edo and Delta: the researcher's mapping)

ledger.note: August 1967: Biafra invades the Mid-West. 'On 9 August, Biafran forces crossed their western border and the Niger river into the Mid-Western state of Nigeria'; the advance reached Benin City in August and stopped at Ore on 21 August. The year is read from the page's 1967 sequence.

region.text: the Mid-Western state (modern Edo and Delta: the researcher's mapping)

ledger.note: 22 September 1967: Nigeria retakes the Mid-West. 'Benin City was retaken by the Nigerians on 22 September'; the Biafran administrator's 'Republic of Benin' (declared 19 September) 'ceased to exist the next day'.

region.text: Enugu, taken by the Nigerian 1st Division

ledger.note: 4 October 1967: Nigerian troops take Enugu. 'On 4 October, the Nigerian 1st Division captured Enugu'; Ojukwu moved his government to Umuahia. The year follows from the page's 12 September 1967 sentence on the plan to take Enugu; a 50 km radius stands for the city and its surroundings.
19 May 1968: Port Harcourt falls. 'On 19 May 1968 Port Harcourt was captured.' The 50 km radius stands for the city and the Niger Delta port area; the page gives no further extent.

minus.text: the Eastern Region, which Ojukwu 'renamed ... the Republic of Biafra' (modern states Abia, Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bayelsa, Cross River, Ebonyi, Enugu, Imo and Rivers: the researcher's mapping)

union.text: Enugu, taken by the Nigerian 1st Division

region.text: the remainder of the Eastern Region after Enugu and Port Harcourt had been retaken

ledger.note: 15 January 1970: Biafra ends and Nigeria is reunited. Infobox: '6 July 1967 - 15 January 1970', result 'Dissolution of the Republic of Biafra and Republic of Benin; Reunification of Nigeria'. The page gives no area for Biafra's last months, so this event returns the rest of the Eastern Region.

12 December 1991: the capital moves from Lagos to Abuja. Abuja 'replaced Lagos (the most populous city in Nigeria) as the capital on 12 December 1991'; Decree No. 6 of 4 February 1976 had begun the move.

wars.outcome: Nigerian victory on 15 January 1970: Biafra and the short-lived Republic of Benin dissolved and Nigeria was reunified.
wars.note: 'The war began in the early hours of 6 July 1967 when Nigerian Federal troops advanced in two columns into Biafra.' Fronts: Mid-West 9 August - 22 September 1967; Enugu 4 October 1967; Port Harcourt 19 May 1968. 'Only five countries (Tanzania, Gabon, Ivory Coast, Zambia, and Haiti) officially recognised the new republic'; Gabon and Ivory Coast did so in May 1968.

certainty.note: Judgment: the pages opened give lengths of the Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon borders but no boundary instruments. The Lake Chad water boundary and the 1967-1970 Biafran front are soft; the Bakassi frontier with Cameroon, disputed until its 2008 settlement, is not covered by the pages opened.

sources.note: Added by the af-08-h reviewer: plebiscite 11 February 1961; Northern Cameroons became the Sardauna Province of Northern Nigeria on 1 June 1961; Southern Cameroons joined Cameroon on 1 October 1961.

notes: Budget: 3 pages (state, civil war, Abuja for the capital date), one over the brief's 1-2 for a state of 3 shapes, offset by the 1-page states of this batch. Not opened (out of page budget): Bakassi (cession to Cameroon in 2008; about 1,000 km2, not drawn at map scale) and British Cameroons for the month of the Northern Cameroons' union; a gap-filler should open 'Bakassi' and 'British Cameroons'. Cliopatria draws pre-1961 Nigeria in the row 'British Gold Coast' (a British West Africa composite) and omits it from 'British Africa' 1956-1960, so Nigeria's colonial counterpart is british-gold-coast. Biafra: no Cliopatria row and no dossier yet. The ledger uses counterpart 'biafra' for the loss, the Mid-West occupation and the three gains; the rebel dossier (type rebel, 1967-1970) belongs to the additions batch af-08-x or to a gap-filler. The Eastern Region and Mid-West regions are admin-1 unions of modern states, the researcher's mapping; Enugu and Port Harcourt are 50 km radii. Gabon and Ivory Coast recognised Biafra in May 1968 (Civil War page). Gazetteer name needed: 'Northern Cameroons'. Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon are the neighbours in the seed.
